title: the seasons
hook: Krishna names spring as his season of flowers; Charaka's spring is also a thaw

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons, and Charaka's winter: a strong inner fire held in by the cold, fed with warm, substantial food. Did you meet the weather with its opposite? Day one thousand three hundred three.

Of the seasons, the one that brings flowers. That's Krishna speaking in the Bhagavad Gita, paraphrased, in a chapter where he names, in kind after kind of thing, where his glory shows: among rivers, among mountains, among months. And among the seasons he chooses spring. So in the Gita, spring arrives already crowned. Blossom, color, the year waking up. But Ayurveda's classical texts read the same season with a second eye, and what they see isn't only flowers. It's a thaw. Today, spring, both ways.
screen: `OF SEASONS, THE ONE THAT BRINGS FLOWERS.` → `SPRING, ALREADY CROWNED.` → `A SECOND EYE: A THAW.`

segments.voice: The Gita's word is kusumakara, the flower-bringer. That's spring as poetry and as worship. Now Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls spring vasanta, and its reading, paraphrased, goes like this. Through the winter, kapha builds up in the body, the heavy, cool, steady quality. Then the spring sun arrives and melts it, the way sun melts snow, and the melting stirs things up. The digestive fire that was so strong in winter gets dampened. People feel heavy, slow, congested. So the advice turns. Avoid foods that are heavy, sour, sweet and rich. Don't sleep through the day. Move: exercise, a brisk rub of the skin. Lighter grains. And, nicely, time in gardens and woods, where spring is doing its flowering. Hold the two readings side by side. First, one season, two pictures, and both are true. The tree blossoms. The yard is mud. A text of devotion can see the first; a text of health insists on the second. Second, the advice is a reversal of yesterday's. What winter asked for, spring asks you to lay down. The seasons don't hand out one diet for the year. Third, the festival calendar runs alongside. In parts of India spring brings Vasant Panchami, when Saraswati is honored, and Holi, with its colors thrown in the open air. Out of the house, into the light, moving. The thaw and the blossom, together.
screen: `KUSUMAKARA, A STOREHOUSE OF FLOWERS` · `WINTER'S KAPHA MELTS` · `LIGHTER FOOD, MORE MOVEMENT` · `ONE SEASON, TWO PICTURES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something thaw. Sit tall, as if a thread drew you up from the crown of the head. Notice any heaviness: in the shoulders, the jaw, the eyelids. Let three exhales be a little longer than the inhales, and on each one let a heavy place soften, the way snow goes soft in the sun. Then just sit, upright and light. If you pray, you can hold one flower in mind, offered. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. In spring, two readings together: the Gita's season of flowers, and Charaka's thaw that asks for lighter food and more movement. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Today, if you feel heavy, choose one lighter thing: a walk instead of a nap, a lighter lunch, a window opened. Day one thousand three hundred three.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat lighter in spring, avoid daytime sleep and move more, as the classical texts advise, and Hindu communities in parts of India mark the season with Vasant Panchami and Holi.

fork.setup: spring sun is melting what winter piled up, and you feel heavy and slow. what does Charaka advise?
options: keep eating the rich winter meals.
fork.reveal: Charaka warns against heavy, sour, sweet, rich food and day sleep in spring, and recommends exercise, lighter grains and time in gardens and woods.

original.note: Sanskrit: kusumakara, the flower-bringer. The Gita's word for spring (10.35).

trapdoor: what you thought: spring is all blossom.
what it means: in Charaka's reading, spring is also the thaw, when winter's kapha melts and slows the body.
what a scholar hears: Gita 10.35's kusumakara set beside Charaka Sutrasthana 6's spring regimen.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.35 (among the seasons, Krishna is kusumakara, the flower-bringing spring)

Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6 (vasanta: kapha accumulated in winter liquefied by the sun; avoid heavy, sour, sweet, unctuous food and day sleep; exercise, rubbing, lighter grains, gardens and forests)

notes: Gita 10.35: confirm 'ṛtūnāṁ kusumākaraḥ' and the paraphrase 'of the seasons, the one that brings flowers'; confirm the chapter's other categories named in the hook (rivers, mountains, months) all appear in Gita 10.
kusumakara glossed as kusuma 'flower' + akara 'source, storehouse, mine': confirm.

Charaka Sutrasthana 6 spring regimen: confirm kapha liquefied by the spring sun, the weakened fire, and the list of what to avoid and do (including udvartana, 'a brisk rub of the skin', and gardens/forests).
'In parts of India spring brings Vasant Panchami ... and Holi': confirm wording.
